summary: Explores how Type-of-Service might be implemented in the Internet by describing a queuing method that can give different classes of service. It also prevents one class from using too many resources or shutting out others. It is an idea paper and discussion is encouraged.

eli5.summary: At a busy checkout, some customers need to be quick and others can wait. This memo suggests a line system that serves each kind fairly without letting any group hog the cashier.

questions: how can queuing provide type of service
what is a queuing algorithm for ip type-of-service
how can a router implement type of service
subtitle: A queuing algorithm that implements Type-of-Service classes for IP networks.

tldr.problem: IP has a Type-of-Service field for low delay, high throughput, and high reliability, but there is no defined mechanism to actually deliver these different service levels.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes separate queues for each service class with different sizes and service rates. Low delay traffic gets a small queue and high service rate, while high throughput gets a larger queue and highest rate, and high reliability gets an even larger queue.
tldr.outcome: Networks can enforce different service levels using a fair queuing approach that prevents any class from starving others while respecting priorities.

facts.label: Service classes
facts.value: Low delay, high throughput, high reliability

facts.label: Maximum Guaranteed Delay
facts.value: Per node, worst-case is MGD times number of hops

today: RFC 1046 was an early exploration of Quality of Service (QoS) implementation. While this specific algorithm was not widely adopted, the concepts influenced later QoS standards like Differentiated Services (DiffServ), which also use multiple service classes and per-hop behaviors. Modern networks implement QoS through various mechanisms including weighted fair queuing, traffic policing, and priority queuing.

sections.title: The Type-of-Service Field
sections.content:
The IP header includes a Type-of-Service (TOS) field that lets senders request low delay, high throughput, or high reliability. It also includes a priority level from 0 to 7. However, the original IP specification did not define what routers should do with this information. This RFC proposes a concrete queuing algorithm to actually implement these service levels.

The three service classes represent different application needs: an interactive terminal session needs low delay; a bulk file transfer wants high throughput; and a critical business application wants high reliability (low loss).
sections.eli5: IP lets you ask for what you need, but nobody has defined how to actually give it to you. This is a plan to do that.

sections.title: The Three-Queue Architecture
sections.content:
The algorithm uses three separate queues: one for low delay traffic, one for high throughput, and one for high reliability. Each queue has different properties.

The low delay queue is small, so packets spend minimal time waiting. It is serviced at a low percentage of the available bandwidth (for example, 17%), ensuring that low delay traffic does not consume excessive resources. Packets that arrive when the queue is full are discarded immediately rather than waiting.

The high reliability queue is longer, allowing packets to wait rather than be lost. It is serviced at a medium rate (for example, 33%) and sends flow control messages (Source Quench) earlier than normal, before the queue fills completely.

The high throughput queue is the largest and gets the most bandwidth (for example, 50%). It operates like normal IP queuing. Datagram streams are grouped together when possible to improve overall performance.
sections.eli5: Three separate lines: a short express line for urgent packets, a medium line for reliable delivery, and a long line for bulk data. Each line gets a fair share of the router's processing power.

sections.title: Service Rates and Fair Allocation
sections.content:
Rather than simply serving queues in order, the algorithm allocates time slots across service cycles. In each cycle, the low delay queue gets allocated time to send its allotted percentage of packets, then high reliability, then high throughput. Unused bandwidth from one class can be reallocated to others.

To prevent the low delay queue from consuming excessive bandwidth despite its small size, the algorithm uses a chit-based credit system. Each service interval, each queue receives credits proportional to its allocated percentage. Queues spend credits as they send packets. If a queue does not spend all its credits, they can carry over partially to the next cycle, allowing bursty traffic to be served smoothly.

This approach ensures that each class gets its promised minimum bandwidth, prevents starvation, and prevents any single class from monopolizing the router.
sections.eli5: Each second, the router divides its time into thirds: 17% for express, 33% for reliable, 50% for bulk. If express doesn't use all its time, it doesn't get wasted—the next second starts fresh.

sections.title: Priority within Classes
sections.content:
Packets can specify a priority level from 0 to 7 in addition to their service class. High-priority packets are queued ahead of lower-priority packets within their queue. To prevent low-priority packets from being permanently starved, the algorithm uses frustration points: each time a packet is preempted by a higher-priority packet, its priority is locally raised. This ensures that even a priority 0 packet will eventually get through within a few hops.

The implementation uses a simple multiplier scheme: multiply the priority by 2 or 4 and increment it each time the packet is preempted. Within a few preemptions, the packet's local priority rises enough that it will no longer be preempted at that hop.
sections.eli5: Important packets jump ahead in line, but if you've been waiting a long time and important packets keep cutting in, you eventually jump ahead too. Nobody waits forever.

sections.title: Applicability and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The algorithm is designed for use in routers when queue buildup becomes a problem—it need not be active when traffic is light. When traffic is heavy enough that multiple queues form, the algorithm can be turned on to provide the promised service levels.

A simplified implementation could provide just the low delay queue, which would immediately improve interactive performance without implementing the full algorithm. The main trade-off is complexity: the algorithm adds processing overhead to the router, but as Dave Clark noted in the RFC, this overhead is reasonable compared to total packet processing time.

The algorithm assumes that the application sets TOS dynamically based on the current data being sent, not on a per-session basis. Some protocols like TCP might benefit from adjusting TOS based on the amount of data being sent in each transmission.
sections.eli5: You only need this when traffic gets heavy. A simple version with just the express line would help right away. It adds some work to the router, but not much.
